title: Security review: admin activity telemetry, retention & KMS - Orpheus Health
summary: Orpheus Health asked for a focused walkthrough of what Redwood captures for admin and audit trails, export and retention capabilities, and how KMS/HSM integrations and key management affect log visibility and legal hold. Agreed next steps: share SOC 2 artifact packet, KMS integration guide, and a small export sample (NDJSON) + schedule a follow-up with their SIEM team.
topics: What admin actions/events are logged (user authentications, role changes, key access)
Export options: S3, syslog, NDJSON batch and streaming webhooks
Retention and legal hold / immutability policies
KMS/HSM integration details and key rotation effects on log decryption
RBAC/SSO interplay for who can see admin trails
action_items: Jordan Patel: send SOC 2 summary + evidence pack (due 2025-03-14)
Sofia Martinez: produce sample audit export (NDJSON) with an example admin-change event (due 2025-03-17)
Derek O'Neill (Orpheus): share SIEM contact and preferred ingestion method (due 2025-03-18)
next_steps: Redwood to email KMS integration guide and HSM FAQ
Schedule follow-up with Orpheus SIEM engineer to validate syslog/ S3 ingest
Provide retention/immutability SLA language for legal review
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan Patel: hey everyone thanks for taking the time, this is Jordan from Redwood — I'm AE on the account. today we're narrowing in on admin telemetry and audit logs, especially retention and KMS.
[00:00:18] Mark Rivers: thanks Jordan. quick context — we run a hybrid setup, some PHI-adjacent data, so audit trails and immutability are must haves for compliance. we're particularly concerned about who can view and export admin logs.
[00:00:35] Sofia Martinez: hi Mark, Lina, Derek — Sofia here. i'll start with what we capture. high level: we log authentication events (SSO/SAML successes and failures), role and permission changes, API key operations (create/revoke), model deployment actions, rollback/canary events, and access to sensitive endpoints like audit exports. also system-generated events: autoscale changes and routing fallbacks.
[00:01:05] Lina Chen: when you say "access to audit exports" does that mean you log who downloads an export, and from where?
[00:01:13] Sofia Martinez: yes — we log the user identity, the IP, timestamp, export job id, and the destination (s3 bucket or syslog target). often the export is initiated by a user in the console or via API; both are captured.
[00:01:30] Derek O'Neill: is that export encrypted? like, if it lands in our s3, is Redwood applying server-side encryption or is it plaintext?
[00:01:37] Jordan Patel: good q. exports are delivered raw — Redwood doesn't re-encrypt destination buckets. we support SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS recommendations in docs; customers should configure their destination bucket with their chosen SSE. we also support signed pre-signed URLs with short TTLs for direct download.
[00:01:55] Mark Rivers: hmm ok. we want envelope encryption — where logs are encrypted with a key we control. how does Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
[00:02:03] Sofia Martinez: we support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) for server-side encryption of objects Redwood stores. for private deployments we can integrate with an on-prem HSM; there is an operational playbook. note: if you enable CMK and key rotation, audit logs referencing key IDs remain, but ciphertext blobs require the active key to decrypt if we stored anything encrypted. typical pattern: Redwood writes logs encrypted with envelope keys, and customers keep control of the master key.
[00:02:36] Lina Chen: wanted to clarify — are the logs Redwood keeps in their control plane encrypted with keys we manage, or only the exported copies?
[00:02:44] Sofia Martinez: both options exist for Private deployments. for Hosted we offer customer-managed keys for stored artifacts (including logs) via our KMS integration. for Hosted SaaS, the control plane metadata (e.g., policy decisions) is also logged but sensitive payloads are redacted unless you enable pay-per-customer encryption.
[00:03:03] Derek O'Neill: if we rotate keys, do old logs become unreadable? we have legal retention and e-discovery needs.
[00:03:11] Sofia Martinez: rotation is a common concern. we recommend a key-rotation window where we re-encrypt historical objects with the new data key before retiring old keys. for very large archives we provide a re-encryption job that can run asynchronously — it can take time, depends on volume. alternatively you can export to your bucket and manage retention/rotation there.
[00:03:32] Mark Rivers: what about immutability/legal holds? can you set WORM or object lock on exports?
[00:03:39] Jordan Patel: Redwood doesn't toggle object lock on your S3 destination automatically, but we can wire the export job to set object metadata which your ingestion pipeline can use to apply object lock or retention in the destination. for private deployments we can support direct object lock if the storage supports it.
[00:03:59] [00:04:00] Speaker 4: (inaudible)
[00:04:15] Lina Chen: on RBAC: who in our org can request an export? is there fine-grained permissions?
[00:04:22] Sofia Martinez: yes — RBAC is per-route and per-action. roles are configurable: viewer, auditor, admin, security_officer, and custom roles. only roles with the export permission can generate exports. also exports can be gated behind approval flows where two people need to approve.
[00:04:41] Derek O'Neill: does the audit trail capture approval steps too?
[00:04:44] Sofia Martinez: yes every step is an event in the trail — request, approver id, timestamps, decision. those events include both user principal and SSO assertion details (e.g., Okta user id, SAML assertion id).
[00:04:58] Mark Rivers: we use Okta and have SAML SSO enabled. how do you correlate SSO identities with audit records?
[00:05:04] Jordan Patel: we persist the SAML subject/Okta user id and map to internal ids. in the export you'll see both the internal "userId" field and the external identity provider fields. sometimes the transcription on our old transcripts says "S O M L" but to be clear it's SAML.
[00:05:21] Lina Chen: format of exports? CSV? JSON? stream?
[00:05:25] Sofia Martinez: default is NDJSON per-line JSON objects — easier for SIEM ingestion. we can also do CSV for ad-hoc. export delivery options: S3 (batch), syslog (streaming), webhook/HTTP PUT for near-real-time. batch exports are zipped and include a manifest.
[00:05:45] Derek O'Neill: SIEMs expect syslog or raw JSON. latency of streaming — how near real-time is webhook/syslog?
[00:05:52] Sofia Martinez: webhooks are under 5s under normal load; syslog latency typically sub-1s for events. batch exports are hourly/daily depending on retention bucket you pick.
[00:06:06] Mark Rivers: retention policies — what are the default and max retention for audit trails in hosted?
[00:06:11] Jordan Patel: hosted default is 90 days for admin-level detailed logs, 365 for summarized metrics. we offer extended retention add-ons up to 7 years for enterprise customers with dedicated storage. private deployments are fully configurable.
[00:06:26] Lina Chen: do you offer immutability guarantees for hosted logs? we need tamper-evidence for SOC 2 and for forensics.
[00:06:33] Sofia Martinez: we provide append-only log stores with cryptographic chaining metadata (hash chains) for tamper detection; we timestamp and sign every chunk. that gives tamper evidence. for legal immutability (WORM), we recommend exporting to your own storage with object lock and we provide the signed manifests and chain proofs.
[00:06:51] Derek O'Neill: what about access controls on Redwood's side? who at Redwood can see raw logs?
[00:06:57] Jordan Patel: minimal access. we operate under least privilege: only site reliability and security engineers with explicit approval can access raw logs and every access is audited and captured in a separate access audit trail. cross-account scoping prevents engineers from casually browsing customer logs.
[00:07:15] Mark Rivers: can you show an example event? like an admin role change record?
[00:07:20] Sofia Martinez: sure — i'll paste one in the sample export and in the NDJSON it'll have fields like timestamp, event_type: "role.change", actor: {id, external_id}, target: {id, role}, ip, request_id, correlation_id, sso_assertion_id, raw_payload_redacted:true. we'll include a sample.
[00:07:43] [00:08:00] Jordan Patel: note, some older transcripts occasionally mislabel product names, e.g., "Redwood Dedicated" sometimes becomes "Redwood Dedicated GPU" in speech-to-text. sorry, random aside.
[00:08:12] Lina Chen: are there alerts for suspicious admin activity? can logs feed into Redwood Optimize for anomaly detection?
[00:08:18] Sofia Martinez: yes — we have a detection engine that can flag anomalous patterns (mass role changes, repeated failed SSO auths, unusual export volume). alerts can trigger webhooks, PagerDuty, or create tickets in your ticketing system. those alert events are also logged and exported.
[00:08:36] Derek O'Neill: concerning KMS again — who holds the metadata for key access? do you log KMS decrypt operations?
[00:08:42] Sofia Martinez: we log KMS API calls (key id, operation type, principal) but we don't store plaintext keys. these KMS call logs are part of the audit trail. if you use a managed KMS, you'll also have KMS access logs on your side.
[00:08:56] Mark Rivers: last compliance question — do you have SOC 2 evidence that shows these controls?
[00:09:01] Jordan Patel: yes — we'll send the SOC 2 artifact pack that includes control descriptions for logging, retention, KMS usage, and third-party attestations.
[00:09:09] Lina Chen: one edge case: if an admin changes roles and then immediately deletes a resource, can we reconstruct the timeline in your logs?
[00:09:16] Sofia Martinez: yes — correlation ids and request traces let you recreate the chain. each action includes parent_request_id so you can stitch events together. we also capture pre-change metadata where possible. there can be s time-lag if re-encryption jobs are pending but the event record remains.
[00:09:35] Derek O'Neill: what's the typical size for daily audit logs for an org our size (200 engineers, mid-volume)?
[00:09:42] Jordan Patel: rough calc — a few GB/day if you include detailed request payloads; if you redact payloads and keep only headers/metadata it's closer to hundreds of MB/day. we'll give you an estimate spreadsheet.
[00:09:58] Mark Rivers: are there any gotchas with data residency? logging locations?
[00:10:03] Sofia Martinez: we can restrict log storage to a region for hosted customers — region lock. for private deployments you control region entirely. exports can be forced to land in a specific cloud region. note: some telemetry (control plane metrics) may be routed to our central telemetry if not in private mode.
[00:10:20] Lina Chen: do you support cross-account IAM roles for S3 exports?
[00:10:24] Jordan Patel: yes — recommended pattern is to create a cross-account role that Redwood assumes with least privilege to write to a prefix. that way customers maintain bucket-level control.
[00:10:34] [00:10:40] Mark Rivers: ok, this is helpful. final ask from legal: want export manifest showing who requested exports for last 6 months. can you produce that?
[00:10:48] Sofia Martinez: yes we can run a scoped query and produce a manifest NDJSON that lists export job id, requester id, timestamp, destination. we'll include IPs and approval ids where applicable.
[00:10:59] Jordan Patel: recap: we'll send SOC2 pack, KMS guide, sample NDJSON export with admin-change event, and schedule a SIEM integration session. next meeting — target week of 2025-03-24.
[00:11:15] Mark Rivers: sounds good, thanks.
[00:11:18] Lina Chen: thanks all.
[00:11:20] Derek O'Neill: thanks.
[00:11:23] [END TRANSCRIPT]
notes: Redwood will not enable object lock in customer S3 by default — customer must configure destination accordingly
Key rotation requires re-encryption job for historical objects; consider exporting to customer-managed bucket for e-discovery
SAML/Okta identity mapping included in every event for traceability
